Abstract

Sustainable aviation fuel is among the most practical near-term routes for aviation decarbonization because it can be used in existing aircraft, engines, and airport fuel systems with limited infrastructure changes while minimizing disruption to the aviation fuel supply chain. This review examines SAF applications in aerospace propulsion systems, focusing on production pathways, aero-engine compatibility, property prediction, and fuel heat sink potential. It compares hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), Fischer–Tropsch (FT), alcohol-to-jet (ATJ), synthesized iso-paraffins (SIP), and power-to-liquid (PtL) fuels in terms of feedstock type, process complexity, product composition, and blending constraints. It also assesses how molecular composition governs density, cold-flow behavior, thermal stability, coking propensity, seal compatibility, and emissions. Recent advances in molecular dynamics, machine learning, spectroscopic analysis, and uncertainty quantification show a shift from empirical estimation toward composition-based prediction, prescreening, and fuel design. For high-thermal-load propulsion systems, SAF is further evaluated as a fuel heat sink in active regenerative cooling. Current evidence points to advantages in thermal stability and low coking tendency, but important gaps remain in transcritical and supercritical heat transfer, pyrolytic heat absorption, wall-material effects, coke deposition, and heat sink capacity modeling across wide operating ranges.

1. Introduction

1.1. Aviation Decarbonization Pressure and the Strategic Significance of SAF

The aviation sector is widely recognized as one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize deeply [1]. Global aviation currently emits about 0.8 billion tons of CO2 annually, accounting for roughly 2–3% of anthropogenic CO2 emissions [2]. With global air traffic projected to grow by about 3.6–5% per year, aviation-related CO2 emissions could rise to 10–11% of global emissions by 2050 unless major changes occur in power generation and energy storage technologies [1].

Against the background of global net-zero targets, the aviation sector is facing increasingly stringent pressure to reduce carbon emissions [1]. Existing reviews generally regard sustainable aviation fuels (SAF), hydrogen fuel cells, advanced batteries, and hybrid electric propulsion as the main technological pathways toward net-zero aviation [1]. Among these pathways, SAF is considered the one most likely to be implemented at scale in the near term and is a key option for aviation decarbonization [3].

SAF refers to renewable liquid fuel prepared from lipid feedstocks, lignocellulosic biomass, municipal solid waste, alcohol intermediates, and synthetic routes based on captured CO2/CO and renewable hydrogen [3]. SAF can reduce life cycle GHG emissions, although the reduction depends strongly on feedstock, conversion route, hydrogen source, electricity mix, and system boundary. Some pathways have been reported to approach an 80% reduction relative to fossil jet fuel [3,4]. In addition, biofuel blending can reduce particle emissions under aircraft engine operating conditions [5].

From a fuel system perspective, the near-term applicability of SAF also depends on whether the finished fuel retains density and energy content characteristics comparable to those of conventional aviation kerosene. ASTM D7566-26 specifies a density range of 775–840 kg m−3 at 15 °C and a minimum net heat of combustion of 42.8 MJ kg−1 for finished aviation turbine fuel containing synthesized hydrocarbons [6]. These requirements are important because comparable density helps maintain fuel volume measurement, tank usage, pumping behavior, and aircraft range without major fuel system redesign, while the minimum net heat of combustion ensures that the gravimetric energy content remains within an acceptable specification window. Representative SAF data support this feasibility. For example, Walkling et al. reported that HEFA-Jet had a net heat of combustion of 43.73 MJ kg−1, compared with 43.1 MJ kg−1 for Jet A, although its density was lower, 0.762 g mL−1 compared with 0.807 g mL−1 for Jet A [7]. This density limitation can be improved through molecular formulation and blending: in the same study, a 30:70 DMCO:HEFA-Jet blend reached a density of 0.780 g mL−1, and a linalool-derived 100% SAF blend reached 0.814 g mL−1, both within the ASTM density range, while maintaining net heat of combustion values close to conventional jet fuel [7]. Although L-Jet was within the ASTM density range, the cited formulation required blending to meet the ASTM distillation slope requirement [7].

Klimczyk et al. [4] noted that one major reason for the strong interest in SAF is that it can provide a feasible pathway for reducing life cycle greenhouse gas emissions without requiring fundamental changes to aircraft or airport infrastructure. Wandelt et al. [8] conducted a meta-review of more than 60 publications. They found that SAF research has expanded from basic fuel production to include feedstock availability, fuel synthesis techniques, life cycle evaluation, policy systems, and economic feasibility. In a comprehensive study on the waste to SAF process, Mariyam et al. [9] also emphasized that these methods are extensively discussed due to their potential to reduce aviation carbon emissions and provide additional routes for resource utilization.

Thus, SAF is important not only because it can reduce life cycle emissions but also because it can be deployed within the current aviation system. Its wider use, however, remains constrained by feedstock availability, production cost, and certification requirements [3].

1.2. Stage-Wise Comparison of SAF with Hydrogen and Electric Propulsion Routes

SAF, hydrogen fuel cells, advanced batteries, and hybrid electric propulsion differ substantially in performance limits, system integration complexity, life cycle environmental impacts and certification requirements [1]. Liquid hydrogen (LH2) has a very high gravimetric energy density, approximately three times that of conventional jet fuel, but its volumetric energy density is very low [10,11]. Leitão et al. [12] stated that both hydrogen combustion and hydrogen fuel cell propulsion need significant redesign at the system level. Their practicality is not only influenced by the fuel properties but also by the airframe integration, tank arrangement, and operational restrictions. Gopalasingam et al. [13] also stressed that the difficulties in component performance, storage safety and high-altitude operation for hydrogen-electric systems restrict their application in the near-term commercial aviation.

Hydrogen use is mainly limited by storage requirements. Hydrogen storage is mainly divided into two categories: physical storage and chemical storage. In physical storage, large onboard tanks are required, which increase aircraft weight and aerodynamic drag, thereby increasing fuel consumption [14]. The Cryoplane project indicates that large hydrogen tanks might result in a 10% fuel-burn penalty [15]. As an alternative, chemical storage such as metal hydrides is also feasible since hydrogen can be stored in solid materials, which can enhance thermal management and safety [1]. Separately, compressed and liquid hydrogen storage systems require materials and protective measures compatible with high pressure, hydrogen embrittlement, and, in the case of LH2, cryogenic temperatures [16]. A study conducted by Gallagher et al. [17] revealed that there are considerable differences in the actual operating energy performance and aircraft compatibility between liquid hydrogen and synthetic SAF. From the viewpoint of energy efficiency, LH2 performs better. Nevertheless, considering airport infrastructure, aircraft modifications, and operational complexity, the practical application of LH2 becomes more challenging. Hydrogen tank performance also has a significant impact on aircraft-level outcomes. These constraints help explain why hydrogen propulsion remains more dependent on aircraft-level redesign and infrastructure transformation than SAF in the near term.

Fully electric aircraft are constrained by low energy density and mass penalties. Compared with liquid hydrocarbon fuels, whose specific energy is much higher, current battery technologies still have far lower gravimetric energy density. Lithium-ion batteries have an energy density of about 250 Wh kg−1, which is approximately 50 times lower than that of conventional Jet A fuel [18]. In addition to lithium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries (SSBs), lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, lithium-air batteries, sodium-ion batteries, potassium-ion batteries, and other alternative metal-ion chemistries are under active investigation to improve energy density. However, they still face major challenges, including limited safety, insufficient discharge power, and inadequate long-term stability [1,19,20].

More direct aircraft-level comparisons also show the mass and volume penalties of battery electric propulsion. For the same reserve energy requirement of 4000 kWh, Wolleswinkel et al. reported that a battery-based system would require 13,300 kg of batteries at 300 Wh kg−1, whereas the Jet A-1 fuel required for the fuel-based reserve system was only 1000 kg; even after including the gas turbine and generator, the total mass of the fuel-based system was 5350 kg [21]. The volume constraint is also significant. In a 19-passenger fully electric commuter aircraft concept, Staack et al. estimated a 3000 kg battery system, corresponding to about 35% of take-off mass, and requiring at least 1.5–2 m3 of volume, comparable to a full wet wing or four slightly enlarged nacelles [22]. In addition, batteries face environmental and operational limitations during flight and ground service. Under the standard atmosphere, the ambient temperature near 11 km is about −56.5 °C [23]. Although aircraft battery packs are thermally controlled and are not necessarily exposed directly to the ambient temperature, the very low external temperature environment at cruise altitude increases thermal management demand and may reduce battery performance if the cell temperature is not maintained within its required operating range [19,23]. Recharging also increases airport turnaround time. Doctor et al. modeled short-haul electric aircraft with a 120 min recharging and turnaround time, compared with 30–60 min for short-haul kerosene aircraft [24]. Charging further requires additional airport-side electricity input; Mukhopadhaya and Graver assumed 15% extra electricity input to account for charging losses [25]. These mass, volume, low-temperature, and recharging constraints remain major barriers to the expansion of battery electric propulsion beyond relatively small aircraft and short-range operations.

Accordingly, the near-term application of fully electric propulsion is expected to remain concentrated in short-range and relatively low-payload aircraft. Large-scale commercial all-electric aviation would require a major step change in battery performance. In addition, batteries also face thermal runaway risks, cooling difficulties, strong dependence on lithium, cobalt, and nickel supply chains, and incomplete recycling systems [1].

Hybrid electric propulsion has the advantage that it does not depend entirely on batteries, as in all-electric systems, and does not require a complete redesign of the propulsion architecture, as in pure hydrogen systems. This gives it better transitional feasibility and greater system flexibility. Ningappa et al. [1] regarded hybrid electric propulsion as a feasible approach to reduce emissions, especially when combined with SAF or hydrogen. The main challenge lies in system complexity, particularly in thermal management. Some parts such as batteries, motors, inverters, fuel cells, or gas turbines may generate thermal loads, which must be managed at the same time. In addition, although hybrid systems can reduce emissions, they do not achieve zero emissions automatically. The actual advantages of hybrid systems are dependent on the particular architecture and energy carrier used [1].

Compared with hydrogen fuel cells, advanced batteries, and hybrid electric propulsion, the main advantage of SAF is its compatibility with existing aircraft and facilities, which makes its implementation more feasible in the near future [4]. Recent industry assessments continue to identify SAF as the primary pathway for decarbonizing existing commercial fleets in the near to medium term because it can be introduced with much lower infrastructure disruption and certification burden [26]. The latest European deployment roadmap for zero-emission aviation also shows that large-scale operation of hydrogen, battery electric, and hybrid electric aircraft requires coordinated progress in airport transformation, refueling or recharging infrastructure, and type certification, which further highlights the relative near-term practicality of SAF [27].

SAF is therefore one of the most realistic decarbonization pathways for the aviation sector at the current stage.

1.3. Life Cycle Emissions Reduction and Sustainability Analysis

Current reviews generally agree that the environmental value of SAF cannot be judged only from tailpipe emissions during combustion but must instead be evaluated within a life cycle assessment framework because its emissions-reduction performance depends primarily on feedstock origin as well as fuel production and conversion processes. Braun et al. [28] reported that the CO2 emitted when SAF is burned in an aero-engine is broadly similar to that of conventional kerosene. Its emissions-reduction potential therefore does not come from a large reduction in direct exhaust emissions, but from differences in carbon sourcing, biomass growth, fuel conversion, and energy inputs along the life cycle.

Ningappa et al. [1] also reported that the carbon dioxide reduction potential of SAF during its life cycle could be as high as 89%. However, this value represents an upper-bound estimate and is influenced by various factors such as the specific feedstocks, processes and system boundaries. Klimczyk et al. [4] similarly noted that the environmental effects of SAF are largely dependent on the pathway and affected by the choice of feedstock, conversion route, hydrogen source, and electricity mix.

According to the ICAO CORSIA system, SAF can be considered an eligible fuel if it results in at least a 10% decrease in the net greenhouse gas emissions compared to the conventional aviation fuel [29]. This system takes into account the sustainability of SAF more comprehensively than merely reducing greenhouse gases, such as the conservation of carbon stocks, land-use changes, permanence of emission reductions, and the preservation of water, soil, air, and ecosystems. Recently, Boerboom et al. [30] introduced a comprehensive climate impact assessment from well-to-wake for SAF, indicating a change in the research toward a wider evaluation of the climatic effects.

From a methodological perspective, life cycle assessment (LCA) of SAF should follow the principles and framework of ISO 14040 and the requirements and guidelines of ISO 14044. ISO 14040 sets out goal and scope definitions, life cycle inventory analysis, life cycle impact assessment, interpretation, reporting, and critical review, whereas ISO 14044 specifies the requirements and guidelines for conducting LCA studies [31,32]. The functional unit and system boundary should be explicitly reported; comparative studies may use cradle-to-gate, well-to-tank, or well-to-wake boundaries. For CORSIA actual life cycle emission values, the functional unit is grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule of fuel produced and combusted in an aircraft engine, expressed on a lower heating value basis (g CO2e MJ−1) [33]. The CORSIA system boundary includes the full supply chain from feedstock production or collection through processing, conversion, transportation, and distribution to fuel combustion in an aircraft engine, corresponding to a well-to-wake perspective [33]. Where co-products are generated, the CORSIA methodology assigns emission burdens by energy allocation based on the lower heating values of products and co-products [33]. Therefore, SAF LCA results should be interpreted together with the declared system boundary, functional unit, allocation method, electricity and hydrogen sources, land-use change treatment, and use of default or actual life cycle emission values [33].

Overall, SAF can achieve substantial life cycle emission reductions, but the magnitude of the benefit is pathway- and assumption-dependent. Direct combustion emissions alone are insufficient for assessing SAF sustainability; feedstock production, energy inputs, conversion processes, allocation methods, and land-use effects must also be considered. Therefore, comparisons among SAF pathways should be based on clearly reported and methodologically consistent life cycle assessment frameworks.

1.4. Cost, Supply Capacity, and Barriers to Large-Scale Deployment

Although SAF emissions-reduction potential is well established, most reviews identify cost, feedstock availability, and certification as the main obstacles to its extensive application [34]. Cost is still the greatest hindrance. Ningappa et al. [1] stated that SAF is about four times more expensive than conventional jet fuel, which makes its general use difficult without governmental policies or market supports. Braun et al. [28] further reported that the production of SAF is still much more costly than fossil jet fuel, while SAF currently accounts for only about 1% of aviation fuel consumption in Europe. At present, SAF has proved to be technically valuable for reducing emissions, but its price is still higher than that of fossil kerosene.

Recent techno-economic studies further show that reported SAF economic metrics vary substantially across production pathways, feedstocks, and process configurations. Santiago et al. [35] compared alcohol-to-jet (ATJ) and Fischer–Tropsch (FT) production strategies in a Brazilian sugarcane-based system. They reported minimum selling prices of 0.85 USD L−1 for ATJ from first-generation (1G) ethanol and 1.10 USD L−1 for gasification–FT using sugarcane residues. The corresponding value for ATJ based on integrated first- and second-generation (1G2G) ethanol was 1.07 USD L−1, compared with 0.54 USD L−1 for fossil-derived aviation kerosene. Yang et al. [36] evaluated hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) and ATJ deployment in China. Their initial unit costs correspond to approximately 3.52 USD L−1 for ATJ and 2.14 USD L−1 for HEFA. The original values were 4.359 and 2.651 USD kg−1, respectively. Under their carbon-neutrality scenario, the modeled 2050 costs decreased to approximately 0.42 USD L−1 for ATJ and 0.53 USD L−1 for HEFA. The original values were 0.52 and 0.66 USD kg−1, respectively. In a waste tire-specific process comparison, Rogachuk and Okolie [37] evaluated two modeled production configurations. They reported minimum fuel selling prices of 0.78 USD L−1 for fast pyrolysis followed by hydroprocessing and 0.66 USD L−1 for gasification–FT. Bhatt et al. [38] reported production costs equivalent to approximately 0.85–1.71 USD L−1 across HEFA, FT, and ATJ pathways. These values were originally reported as 3–6 USD per gasoline gallon equivalent (GGE). HEFA using oil feedstocks had the lowest reported value, equivalent to approximately 0.83 USD L−1 (originally 2.9 USD/GGE).

To facilitate unit-level comparison, values originally reported per kilogram or GGE were converted to USD L−1. The mass-based conversion used a representative Jet A-1 density of 0.808 kg L−1 at 15 °C [14]. For the energy-based conversion, a representative Jet A-1 specific energy of 43.2 MJ kg−1 [14] was used. One GGE was taken as 116,090 Btu, equivalent to approximately 122.48 MJ [39]. These assumptions correspond to approximately 3.51 L of Jet A-1 on an energy-equivalent basis per GGE. Because actual fuel density and specific energy vary among pathways and formulations, all converted values should be regarded as approximate. These studies also reported different economic indicators, including minimum selling price, unit cost, and production cost. Unit conversion therefore does not produce fully harmonized techno-economic estimates. The estimates remain scenario-specific because the studies differ in location, feedstock, price year, scale, system boundary, policy treatment, and economic assumptions. Accordingly, they should be interpreted as illustrative pathway comparisons rather than as a universal price ranking.

Supply-side constraints are also important. Ding et al. [34] identified unstable feedstock supply and the absence of advanced refining facilities as the main causes of the high cost and slow introduction of SAF. Even for the most developed process, HEFA, there are limitations on the available suitable feedstocks. For SAF derived from wastes, Mariyam et al. [9] demonstrated that waste-based processes can achieve both emission reductions and resource circulation, but some practical difficulties exist in feedstock collection, conversion efficiency, and supply chain construction. Recent studies on supply chains have shown that the future introduction will be based not only on the development of pathways but also on feedstock acquisition, logistics, refinery placement, transportation networks, and the overall support from policies in the whole supply system [40].

Certification brings an additional difficulty. Besides the constraints of feedstock and refining, Ding et al. [34] reported that safety certification for new SAF technologies is expensive, time-consuming, and sample-intensive. They also noted that the global harmonization of sustainability certification is still incomplete, and the differences among various certification systems may complicate market access and international recognition. In a meta-review, Wandelt et al. [8] identified economic feasibility, policy frameworks, and supply chain constraints as the main topics in the SAF literature review. Recent economic research indicates that the effect of SAF on aviation decarbonization is influenced by policy regulations and carbon-governance mechanisms, particularly under CORSIA. In this case, the promotion of SAF is not only based on technological progress but also on the economic advantages of its life cycle emission reduction [41].

SAF is now widely accepted from a technical viewpoint, but its extensive use is still restricted by feedstock availability, production cost, permitted blending ratios, certification requirements, and pathway-specific environmental constraints. Hence, the discussion on SAF should not only depend on general policy support but also concentrate on production routes, fuel composition, aero-engine compatibility, property prediction methods, thermal behavior, and system-level emissions. This paper aims to provide an engineering-based understanding of SAF production technologies, aero-engine compatibility, property prediction methods, and fuel heat sink potential in aircraft propulsion systems.

Compared with existing SAF and bio-aviation fuel reviews that mainly emphasize feedstock systems, production pathways, life cycle emissions, techno-economic assessment, certification, and policy development [3,4,8,9], this review focuses on the engineering use of SAF in aerospace propulsion systems. The contribution of this review is threefold. First, it links major SAF pathways with pathway-dependent molecular composition and finished fuel properties. Second, it connects these fuel characteristics with aero-engine compatibility, emissions, material compatibility, and property prediction methods. Third, it provides a dedicated discussion of SAF as a potential fuel heat sink in active regenerative cooling systems for high-thermal load aerospace propulsion applications. This perspective frames SAF not only as a low-carbon drop-in fuel but also as an engineering fuel whose composition, compatibility, predictive characterization, and thermal management behavior must be considered together. Accordingly, the novelty lies not in proposing a new SAF production pathway but in integrating pathway selection with downstream propulsion system compatibility and thermal management requirements.

2. Production Processes and Technological Evolution

2.1. Generational Evolution of Feedstock Systems

SAF feedstock systems have changed from first generation food crops and edible oils to second generation non-food biomass, agricultural and forestry residues, waste oils, and municipal wastes, and third generation algal feedstocks are gaining more attention [42,43]. In addition, non-biological synthetic routes using CO2, renewable electricity, and water are also being discussed as longer-term pathways for synthetic aviation fuel production [14,44]. Mariyam et al. [9], in their systematic review of waste-to-SAF pathways, reported that waste streams have become a major research focus in recent years because they simultaneously offer the potential to reduce the carbon footprint of aviation and improve resource circularity.

2.2. Comparison of Major Production Pathways and Their Technical Characteristics

The main certified and new SAF pathways have differences not only in the source of feedstocks but also in the technological maturity, process complexity, carbon-reduction potential, and practical scalability. As described in Table 1, the main SAF production pathways that have gained considerable interest and entered the ASTM certification system include hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), Fischer–Tropsch (FT) synthesis, alcohol-to-jet (ATJ), synthesized iso-paraffins (SIP), and some other synthetic methods with aromatic supplementation [4].

Among these pathways, HEFA has a high technological maturity and a strong commercial foundation. It is generally considered one of the most important present production methods. The main restriction of HEFA is not its process maturity but the availability of feedstocks. Suitable supplies, especially waste oils and animal fats, are limited and cannot satisfy the long-term fuel requirement of the aviation industry by themselves [4].

The FT route has a wider source of feedstocks such as agricultural residues, forestry residues, and municipal solid waste, which provides it with a greater potential for sustainability than routes depending on scarce lipid resources. The life cycle emission advantage may be increased if renewable electricity is employed to generate the necessary hydrogen [4]. However, the main disadvantage is the lengthy conversion process, large capital expenditure and considerable energy consumption, making it more expensive and complicated to put into practice compared with HEFA [45].

For biomass- and waste-derived FT-SPK, gasification is the key upstream step; after pretreatment and size reduction, solid or heterogeneous carbonaceous feedstocks are converted into syngas, primarily H2 and CO, which is then cleaned and conditioned before Fischer–Tropsch synthesis [46]. Gasifier selection is feedstock-dependent. Fixed-bed, fluidized-bed, and entrained-flow gasifiers impose different requirements on feedstock size, moisture content, composition, and operating pressure; consequently, feedstock heterogeneity and operating conditions affect syngas composition and the H2/CO ratio [46]. Before FT synthesis, the syngas must be cleaned of particulates, tars, sulfur compounds, CO2, nitrogen compounds, chlorine species, and alkali metals, and its H2/CO ratio is commonly adjusted toward approximately 2 for conventional Fischer–Tropsch synthesis [46]. After Fischer–Tropsch synthesis, the resulting long-chain hydrocarbons are hydrotreated and hydrocracked to obtain aviation fuel-range products [46]. This biomass- and waste-derived FT-SPK pathway provides broad feedstock flexibility, but the gasification, syngas-conditioning, synthesis, and upgrading steps also increase capital intensity and constrain overall process efficiency [46].

ATJ pathways originate from alcohol intermediates like ethanol and isobutanol, which can be transformed into jet-range hydrocarbons. As these alcohols can be derived from sugar, starch, and certain cellulosic materials, ATJ provides greater flexibility in the choice of feedstocks. However, its cost is still a problem, mainly due to the existence of many conversion stages and a long energy conversion process [4].

SIP is a specific route producing iso-paraffinic compounds from sugar-containing feedstocks. The process logic is clear, but the feedstock foundation is narrow, and the present certification system permits a maximum blending ratio of only 10% [4].

Under certain settings, FT- and ATJ-based routes may also be associated with power-to-liquid (PtL) or production of e-fuels. As noted by Ozkan et al. [44], PtL converts renewable electricity into hydrogen, which is subsequently reacted with captured CO2 through synthesis processes to produce e-kerosene. This route possesses promising long-term prospects since it can lead to a more closed carbon cycle. However, at present, PtL is still energy-consuming and expensive. Its practicability mainly relies on the availability of cheap renewable electricity, green hydrogen, and concentrated carbon sources [17].

Recent industrial and techno-economic studies have shown that the distinctions between HEFA, FT, ATJ, and PtL are not merely based on the selection of feedstocks. They also indicate various degrees of technological maturity, feasibility of scale-up, and complexity of process integration [26,47]. The State-of-the-Industry report of NREL suggests that HEFA is the only alternative fuel production method with considerable commercial application, whereas some other certified or new routes are still confronted with difficulties such as feedstock transportation, refinery integration, and investment expansion [26]. Uddin et al. [47] further point out that both the life cycle carbon reduction and the minimum selling price of fuel are significantly affected by the source of electricity, hydrogen, and the upstream ethanol production route. Therefore, the competitiveness of the pathways is determined by the entire production process instead of the nominal conversion route alone. Comparative pathway analysis also suggests that different SAF routes exhibit clear trade-offs between cost effectiveness and mitigation potential, with HEFA generally remaining more cost-competitive in the near term while FT and other routes may offer stronger long-term mitigation value under suitable supply and policy conditions [48]. These results indicate that future comparisons among SAF production pathways should consider not only nominal carbon-reduction potential but also technology maturity, process efficiency, and realistic scale-up conditions [26,48].
